reviews.title: Something’s Off with the New Dr Sheth Sunscreen
reviews.body: I don’t like Dr Sheth sunscreen anymore, and this change is disappointing. The previous package I used around three months ago worked really well for me. It blended smoothly, sat comfortably on the skin, and never caused any pilling or white residue. However, the current one behaves very differently. It turns patchy during application and leaves behind visible white particles. No matter how carefully I blend it, it starts flaking and even drips down like dandruff, especially with sweat or movement. I’ve tried applying it on bare skin, over moisturizer, waiting between steps, and changing the quantity—nothing helped. The texture simply doesn’t settle the way it used to. A sunscreen should feel reliable and invisible on the skin. This one no longer does. The contrast between the earlier batch and the current one is very noticeable, which makes me wonder if there has been a formulation or quality change. Sadly, I won’t be repurchasing unless this issue is addressed.

reviews.title: CERTIFICATE OF SUNSCREEN
reviews.body: While Dr. Sheth’s Vitamin C Sunscreen claims SPF 50+ PA++++, it is important to note that the SPF rating is based on in-vivo human testing, whereas the PA++++ rating is derived from in-vitro laboratory testing. PA ratings were originally designed to reflect persistent pigment darkening on human skin (PPD), and using an in-vitro method while displaying a PA++++ label can be misleading to consumers who may assume equivalent in-vivo validation. Without transparent disclosure of in-vivo PPD values or accredited certification details, the PA++++ claim appears more like a marketing representation than a clinically equivalent protection guarantee.
